section_summary: This section contains diplomatic reporting, telegraphic despatches, and State Department memoranda from late December 1938 to mid-January 1939 regarding major political and administrative transitions in Japan. It documents the resignation of Prime Minister Fumimaro Konoe and the installation of the Hiranuma Cabinet, detailing official justifications, underlying factional disputes over totalitarian policies and Admiral Suetsugu, and international editorial reactions from China and the Soviet Union. In addition, it includes Tokyo Despatch No. 3549 and internal State Department commentary transmitting the Imperial Ordinances and personnel appointments that officially established the Asia Promotion Board (Koa-in) to direct Japanese affairs in occupied China.

subfiles.about: Reporting on the background, political factors, and press reactions concerning the resignation of Prime Minister Konoe and the formation of the Hiranuma Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports from Tokyo on the transition from the Konoye Cabinet to the newly formed Hiranuma Cabinet. He notes that the Japanese public accepted Konoye's explanation regarding the completion of the first phase of the China conflict, while a change in leadership was deemed necessary to reinvigorate national enthusiasm. Grew explains that Konoye's resignation was precipitated by parliamentary resistance to Admiral Suetsugu's radical totalitarian measures and proposals for a National Party, which made Suetsugu's continuation in office untenable. The telegram also highlights Prime Minister Hiranuma's public remarks stressing national unity and the subordination of individualism to the state and Imperial Dynasty, while Japanese press editorials dismissed foreign predictions of an immediate turn toward Fascism.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 14 from Tokyo on the Resignation of the Konoye Cabinet and Formation of the Hiranuma Cabinet

subfiles.about: Confidential paraphrase of Tokyo's Telegram No. 14 outlining new Cabinet appointments and analyzing the causes of Konoye's resignation.
subfiles.summary: This confidential paraphrase of Tokyo Telegram No. 14 details the personnel composition of the newly formed Hiranuma Cabinet, listing retained ministers, concurrent portfolio assignments, and new appointees drawn from the bureaucracy and political parties (Seiyukai and Minseito). It examines the causes behind the cabinet reorganization, concluding that the primary factor was the need for a psychological lift in the public attitude toward the China conflict after major hostilities had concluded. It also confirms that political frictions regarding Admiral Suetsugu's totalitarian ambitions and the creation of a National Party forced Konoye's retirement, while quoting Hiranuma's ideological address on national family solidarity and reviewing economic expectations under the new Minister of Finance.
subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Telegram No. 14 of January 6, 1939, from the American Embassy at Tokyo

subfiles.about: Reporting from Chungking on Chinese press editorials and political reactions to the fall of the Konoye Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Peck reports Chungking press read the Konoye Cabinet's fall as Japanese internal difficulty and rising militarism, predicting escalated operations, a hard line on Russia, an Axis alliance and an end to Wang Ching-wei's peace efforts.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 16 from Chungking on Chinese Press Reactions to the Fall of the Konoye Cabinet

subfiles.about: Reporting from Moscow on Soviet press commentary and a Pravda article analyzing the Japanese cabinet change.
subfiles.summary: Kirk summarizes Pravda: the Konoye Cabinet fell over China policy failure and isolation. Hiranuma's accession is a victory for military fascist circles, bringing more aggression and repression.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 12 from Moscow on Soviet Press Comment on the Japanese Cabinet Change

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 3549 regarding the establishment and scope of the Asia Promotion Board.
subfiles.summary: Salisbury summarizes Despatch No. 3549 on the Asia Promotion Board (Koa-in), created December 16, 1938 to run all China affairs, led by military officers, and intended to outlast the hostilities.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 3549 Regarding the Asia Promotion Board (Koa-in)

subfiles.about: Official reporting on the establishment of the Asia Promotion Board (Koa-in), transmitting translations of Imperial Ordinances Nos. 758 and 759 and appointment rosters.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports on the formal organization of the Asia Promotion Board (Koa-in) as Japan's central governmental organ for administering non-diplomatic affairs in China during the conflict. The despatch transmits complete translations of Imperial Ordinance No. 758 setting forth the board's organizational structure, Imperial Ordinance No. 759 governing its affiliated field offices throughout China, and an official list of appointed personnel headed by Lieutenant-General Heisuke Yanagawa as Director General and Major-General Sadaichi Suzuki as Chief of the Political Department. Grew analyzes the dominant authority granted to active-duty military officers, the jurisdictional friction between the board and diplomatic authorities, and official statements indicating that the agency will persist until Japan's envisioned new order in East Asia is fully realized.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3549 from Tokyo: The Asia Promotion Board (Koa-in)
